name: Gray Matter
label: Dischord
lede: Dante Ferrando and Mark Haggerty walked out of Iron Cross, went back to the friends they'd played with since junior high, and made hardcore sing. The band broke up for college, came back, and Ferrando went on to open the Black Cat.

eras.title: Walking out of Iron Cross
eras.text: Gray Matter started as an exit. Dante Ferrando and Mark Haggerty quit Iron Cross when, in Dischord's telling, the band's image began to reflect its violent supporters more than its members. They went back to the friends they'd been playing with since junior high.

years.h: Ferrando and Haggerty walk out of [[Iron Cross|13afe528-54f1-4955-bbec-a4bafb590edb]]
years.p: Drummer [[Dante Ferrando|98b1e2a2-3868-47f0-b905-35637b5a902f]] and guitarist [[Mark Haggerty|235b9917-3f4c-4670-ade3-d94f8e45a044]] leave D.C.'s skinhead-favorite band, uneasy with the crowd it was drawing.

years.h: Before the name stuck, they were the G-men
years.p: [[Geoff Turner|591fc466-2668-4524-852d-a6cc5f18cff7]], [[Steve Niles|ce17b293-3129-426d-b9d3-7403dfda4d8f]], Haggerty and Ferrando played as G-men. Dischord says they'd been making noise together since junior high.

years.big: "We weren't a hardcore band, really. We weren't a thrash band."
years.h: Gray Matter, officially, in summer 1983
years.p: Turner on vocals and guitar, Niles on bass, Haggerty on guitar, Ferrando on drums, all four still in high school. The quote is Turner's own description of the sound.
years.xp:
Dischord dates the official start to the summer of 1983. The Turner, Niles, Haggerty and Ferrando lineup is the one on every Gray Matter record, across two separate runs.

Haggerty has named the Rolling Stones and Janis Joplin as influences, along with the D.C. Food for Thought cafe scene.

The University of Maryland's DC punk archive credits the band with melding hardcore's driving intensity to much more melodic, skillful songwriting.

eras.title: Hardcore that learned to sing
eras.text: While D.C.'s first wave burned out, Gray Matter wrote songs with hooks and cut two records at Inner Ear with Ian MacKaye producing. That put them at the center of the melodic turn later filed under Revolution Summer and post-hardcore.

years.h: Food For Thought lands on R&B Records, not Dischord
years.p: Cut at Inner Ear in November 1984 with [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and Bert Queiroz producing, the debut LP comes out while the band is still in high school.
years.xp:
MacKaye sang backups on the sessions. "Oscar's Eye" would later be Dischord's pick for its 20th-anniversary box.

Dischord's own page is clear that the album first came out on R&B Records in 1985, and only later joined the Dischord catalog as No. 48. The Wikipedia track list also includes a cover of the Beatles' "I Am the Walrus" from the same November 1984 sessions.

The name has a D.C. echo: Food for Thought was also the Dupont Circle vegetarian restaurant run by Dante Ferrando's father, Bobby, from 1973 to 1999, a room that hosted punk shows. No source we found says the album was named for it.

years.h: An early "Walk the Line" turns up on Alive and Kicking
years.p: The WGNS compilation 7" is the band's first link to the studio Turner would go on to run.

yt: On the roof of Food for Thought, 1985
years.h: Back at Inner Ear for six more songs
years.p: MacKaye produces again, and the session includes "Chutes and Ladders" and the seven-minute-plus "Head". That summer the band also plays the roof of Food for Thought, on film.

years.h: Take It Back puts the band on Dischord proper
years.p: Dischord No. 21, a 12" EP. Tight, bright and sung, it's the record fans hand people to explain the band.

years.h: Haggerty leaves for college, and the band ends
years.p: Guitarist Haggerty heads off to school. Ferrando joins [[Ignition|3cb2b7d6-1f0b-4ac5-b67f-52132f3d3b61]].
years.xp:
Dischord's history says Mark Haggerty left for college shortly after Take It Back and the band broke up. Wikipedia dates the split to May 1986.

Wikipedia also lists a second guitarist, [[Jon Kirschten|660b0e16-ab22-49b4-8646-6777c432da4c]], in the band from 1985 to 1986, who went on to form [[Rain|4e9323df-ca77-4e43-addf-bb520fb1b983]]. Dischord's history doesn't mention him.

eras.title: A detour with Jeff Nelson
eras.text: The breakup barely slowed anyone down. Three of the four regrouped with Jeff Nelson of Minor Threat, and for a moment Ian MacKaye too, in a band that pushed D.C. further toward melody.

years.h: Turner and Niles start Three with MacKaye and Nelson
years.p: [[Ian MacKaye|c12f644b-1066-4ead-b0dd-d0c380f5cca2]] and [[Jeff Nelson|51f7994c-949d-4dbe-89eb-2c33f42a5620]] join them, then MacKaye soon leaves. Haggerty steps in on guitar and Turner ends up singing.

years.h: Three's last show is New Year's Day at the 9:30 Club
years.p: The band's only album, Dark Days Coming, comes out on Dischord in 1989.

years.h: Live at DC Space, 1989

eras.title: Back together, then a club of their own
eras.text: Gray Matter came back in 1990 as grown men with a studio of their own, Turner's WGNS, and made their most ambitious record there. When it ended again in 1993, Ferrando opened the Black Cat, the venue that would anchor D.C.'s scene for the next thirty years.

years.h: The 1983 lineup gets back together
years.p: Turner, Niles, Haggerty and Ferrando reform in spring. Dischord also gathers Food For Thought and Take It Back onto one CD that year, No. 49.

years.h: A double seven-inch called 4 Songs
years.p: Dischord and WGNS co-release it. "Bite the Bit" and "October" get new versions on Thog.

years.h: "Second Guess" shares a 7" with [[Severin|4e4b4490-1c10-4e0c-b794-afa4688f88a6]]
years.p: It's a Dischord/Superbad split, with Gray Matter on one side and Severin on the other. Haggerty would join Severin later.

years.h: Thog is cut at Turner's own WGNS
years.p: Eleven songs, produced by the band. Dischord No. 68, and out of print on CD and LP for years.

years.h: The second run ends
years.p: Turner keeps producing at WGNS, and Niles is already writing comics.

years.h: Ferrando opens the Black Cat
years.p: The club's first show is by 9353. Ferrando built it with investors that included [[Dave Grohl|4d5f891d-9bce-45ae-ad86-912dd27252fa]].
years.xp:
Ferrando named the club after a place his great-grandfather ran in Greenwich Village in the 1920s. Its café served mostly vegetarian food and was named Food for Thought, after his father Bobby's Dupont Circle restaurant.

For DC punk it meant a home. Anniversaries at the Black Cat would become the only reliable way to see Gray Matter again.

eras.title: The house band for birthdays
eras.text: Gray Matter never quite reunited, and never quite went away. Every five years the Black Cat throws itself a party, and the original four show up for it.

years.h: The Black Cat's 10th anniversary turns into a habit
years.p: Billed as a one-off, it isn't: the band returns for the club's 15th, 20th, 25th and 30th anniversaries too.

years.h: Dischord remasters the early records
years.p: Food For Thought and Take It Back on one CD, still No. 49.

years.h: 30 Days of Night reaches theaters
years.p: The film of Niles's vampire comic with Ben Templesmith opens. Niles started out self-publishing through Arcane Comix.

years.h: Reunion at the Black Cat's 15th anniversary, September 12, 2008
yt: Reunion at the Black Cat's 15th anniversary, September 12, 2008
"Take It Back" at the Black Cat, 2023
years.h: Take It Back grows to ten songs on blue vinyl
years.p: Food For Thought and Take It Back are re-cut on vinyl, with the four songs from 4 Songs added to Take It Back.
